name: Cruise phase

card.summary: The lower-intake stretch between higher-intake "blast" phases in anabolic steroid use, discussed by users as a way to hold onto muscle and fullness of physique between peaks.
card.note: Involves prescription-only hormones; long-term anabolic steroid use is linked to cardiovascular, hormonal and other harms.

quick.overview:
In bodybuilding and looksmaxxing forums, a cruise is the period between "blasts" in which a person stays on a lower, steady level of testosterone-type hormone instead of coming off entirely. Users describe it as a way to keep the muscle, strength and leaner look gained during a blast while giving the body a lower-intake period.

A muscular, lean physique is a core appearance goal in the community. Forum posters present cruising as part of long-term programmes meant to maintain that physique. Research on anabolic steroids describes strong effects on muscle but also documented harms, and controlled studies of blast-and-cruise schedules are not available.
quick.how: Posters describe alternating a short higher-intake blast with a long lower-intake cruise, often on a testosterone base, sometimes for years, with regular blood tests. Specifics are individual and are not detailed here.
quick.risks: Anabolic steroids are controlled or prescription-only in many countries. Clinicians report cardiovascular strain, adverse cholesterol changes, liver and kidney effects, suppressed natural testosterone, infertility, acne, hair loss and psychiatric effects with prolonged use.

lead: Cruise phase refers to the lower-intake period that follows a blast in a "blast and cruise" pattern of anabolic steroid use. Instead of stopping entirely between blasts, the user continues a steady lower level, which proponents say preserves muscle and a physique they have built. A bodybuilding commentator describes the approach as skipping the off-cycle break and keeping the user on steroids year-round, alternating a heavy phase with a low phase [3].

Maintaining muscle mass and leanness is the appearance link: a fuller, more muscular frame is a central goal for many looksmaxxers. One long forum thread titled as a ten-year blast-and-cruise case study describes a steady base between blasts of several compounds and reports normal bloodwork, full hair, a clear cardiac calcium score and no heart enlargement, while the poster states the thread is not meant to glamorise use and acknowledges obvious risks [1].

Published medical sources describe steroid effects differently. Wikipedia's overview of anabolic steroids lists changes in cholesterol, raised blood pressure, left ventricular thickening and greater risk of heart attack, stroke and sudden cardiac death, liver damage with high oral doses, kidney scarring in a study of bodybuilders, suppression of natural testosterone, and dependence and psychiatric effects [2]. No controlled trial has compared blast-and-cruise schedules with other patterns.

chain: Steady lower hormone level between blasts
angle.text: Users say a cruise keeps the size and definition gained in a blast rather than losing it between cycles. The claim comes from forum and bodybuilding-community experience and has not been tested in controlled trials.

infobox: Anabolic steroids are controlled or Rx-only in many countries (US Schedule III, UK Class C) [2]
Testosterone replacement therapy for diagnosed hypogonadism [4]

paras: In steroid-use vocabulary a blast is a higher-intake phase aimed at adding size, and a cruise is the long, lower, steady phase around it. Traditional "cycles" end with a break from the drugs; blast and cruise replaces the break with a continuing lower level and a return to a blast later [3]. Forum accounts describe running cruises for years with brief blasts on top [1].

The pattern is discussed in bodybuilding media as a more modern practice than the on-off cycles associated with earlier eras of the sport [3]. The exact date and originator of the term are not documented in the sources reviewed. The practice sits within a longer history: testosterone was isolated in 1935 and approved for medical use in 1939, and anabolic steroids spread through bodybuilding and sport from the 1950s, becoming common in the 1970s and moving into the general population after 1980 according to one narrative review [4][5].

A terminology shift has been noted by former bodybuilder and YouTuber Seth Feroce, who said in a January 2024 Fitness Volt report that athletes now describe regimens as blasting or "TRT" rather than cruising, and that a person just off a cycle on a low dose is not on TRT in the medical sense [6]. In medicine, testosterone replacement therapy means treating diagnosed hypogonadism to keep levels in the normal male range, which Wikipedia contrasts with non-medical use aimed at performance or physique [4].

A looksmax.org poster describes ten years on this pattern and says he retained much more muscle than an identical twin at the same body-fat level, even after a period at a markedly lower dose, and presents it as a case study because such reports are scarce on the forum [1]. Replies in comparable threads question why anyone would stack the large combinations described.

Researchers note that most non-medical users are recreational lifters motivated by appearance rather than competitive athletes, and that the internet is the main acquisition route [5]. One survey cited on Wikipedia found 78.4 percent of users were noncompetitive bodybuilders or non-athletes [2].

A 2023 report by the Center for Countering Digital Hate, covered by TechCrunch, found videos using hashtags for steroid-like drugs (steroids, peptides and SARMs) drew more than 580 million views from US users over three years, mostly from men aged 18 to 24, and identified 35 TikTok influencers with ties to sellers and about 1.8 million combined followers [7]. The report's CEO called it a failure of TikTok to enforce its rules [7].

Psychology researchers Timothy Piatkowski and Samuel Cornell wrote in 2025 that Instagram and TikTok present steroids as a quick fix, that sculpted influencer physiques set standards many cannot reach, and that some influencers offer drug coaching under a harm-reduction model. They argue education is more effective than shaming [8]. A narrative review likewise links image-focused platforms to body-image dissatisfaction and steroid use among young men [5].

General medical sources list cardiovascular, hepatic, renal, hormonal and psychiatric adverse effects of prolonged anabolic steroid use [2]. Suppression of natural testosterone can lead to testicular shrinkage, reduced sperm production and infertility, though after a short course a recovery therapy usually restores production [2]. Breast tissue growth, acne and hair loss are also reported [2][5].

A commentary by bodybuilding writer Jerry Brainum, reported by Generation Iron, argues that removing the off-cycle break gives the liver no chance to recover and says blasting and cruising is more dangerous than a standard cycle; the article cites no specific studies for that comparison and says liver changes from cycles are usually recoverable [3]. Wikipedia notes that the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies anabolic steroids as probably carcinogenic to humans (Group 2A) [2].

No study has compared blast-and-cruise schedules with other patterns, so the heart findings below concern long-term users in general. In a 2010 Circulation: Heart Failure study, 12 long-term steroid-using weightlifters had lower left ventricular ejection fraction than 7 non-using weightlifters (median 50.6 percent versus 59.1 percent) and signs of impaired relaxation; the authors called it a small exploratory cross-sectional study needing confirmation [9].

A 2023 Norwegian study in the European Journal of Preventive Cardiology compared 101 weightlifting steroid users (69 current, 30 former) with 71 non-using weightlifters. Users had lower ejection fraction (49 percent versus 59 percent) and higher left ventricular mass, and about 11 percent had ejection fraction at or below 40 percent, with similar rates in current and former users; the design cannot establish causation [10]. Separate follow-up reporting has described partial improvement in some users who stopped, so findings on reversibility differ between studies.

No studies found on blast-and-cruise schedules themselves. Related observational research on long-term anabolic steroid users and the heart is described above [9][10]; the largest randomized testosterone-replacement trial, TRAVERSE, enrolled men with diagnosed hypogonadism and reported no increase in adverse cardiovascular outcomes, which concerns medical replacement rather than physique-oriented use [4].

timeline.event: Testosterone is approved for medical use [4].
Anabolic steroid use begins spreading through bodybuilding and sport [5].
Use becomes common among bodybuilders and athletes [5].
Testosterone and anabolic steroids become controlled substances in the United States [4].
Circulation: Heart Failure study reports reduced left ventricular function in long-term steroid-using weightlifters [9].
CCDH report documents steroid-like drug promotion on TikTok; Norwegian cardiomyopathy study published online [7][10].
Seth Feroce comments on the shift from "cruise" to "TRT" language [6].
Researchers write about social media driving young men's steroid use; the ten-year blast-and-cruise forum case study is posted [8][1].

lore.intro: Posters present cruising as a sustainable way to maintain results, while acknowledging risks [1]. In wider bodybuilding media the practice is discussed both as routine and as a concern [3][6].

claims.claim: A steady cruise retains muscle between blasts better than coming off
claims.believers: A ten-year user reports holding more muscle and strength than his twin at similar body fat after dropping to a low dose [1].
claims.experts: No published trial has tested blast-and-cruise schedules; reviews describe adverse effects of prolonged use [2].

claims.claim: Long-term users with good bloodwork do not suffer the usual harms
claims.believers: The poster reports clear cardiac scores, no heart enlargement and no liver tumours [1].
claims.experts: Medical overviews document cardiovascular, liver, kidney and hormonal harms from prolonged use [2]; echocardiography studies of long-term users found reduced ejection fraction versus non-using lifters [9][10].

claims.claim: A low cruise dose is effectively the same as TRT
claims.believers: Some bodybuilders describe the lower phase as TRT, a framing used on social media [6].
claims.experts: Medicine defines TRT as treatment of diagnosed hypogonadism to restore normal levels, distinct from non-medical use [4]; Feroce himself says a post-cycle low dose is not TRT [6].

claims.claim: Staying on year-round removes the recovery that off-cycle breaks give
claims.believers: Critics in bodybuilding media say continuous use denies the liver time to repair [3].
claims.experts: The commentary cites no specific studies for the comparison, and no controlled trial compares the patterns [3].

claims.claim: Social media shows what a natural physique looks like
claims.believers: Followers often take influencer physiques at face value.
claims.experts: Researchers say some influencers presented as natural have later been exposed as users, which can make steroids seem necessary [8].
